title: al-ʿAwāmil al-jadīda
author: al-Birgivī
subject: nahw
summary: The first book of naḥw in the Ottoman madrasa, by Meḥmed Birgivī of Birgi (d. 981/1573), read after the ṣarf primers and before his Iẓhār al-asrār. It lays out the whole of iʿrāb as a hundred things to know: sixty governors (ʿawāmil), thirty governed words (maʿmūlāt) and ten signs of iʿrāb, in three short chapters, and nearly every example teaches a point of belief or conduct as well as grammar. The lessons take the governors kind by kind, then the governed words and the signs, explaining each rule on Birgivī's own sentences and comparing it with al-Ājurrūmiyya where the two books differ.

lessons.title: A hundred things: governors, governed, iʿrāb
body: Birgivī opens with a promise and a number: whoever wants to know iʿrāb must know a hundred things. Sixty are governors (ʿāmil), the words or ideas that cause an ending; thirty are governed words (maʿmūl), the words whose endings are caused; ten are the effect itself, the signs of iʿrāb. The whole of naḥw at this level is a matter of cause and effect: a governor acts on a governed word, and the ending is what it does.

The book is called al-ʿAwāmil al-jadīda, “the new ʿAwāmil”, because the madrasa already read an older book of governors, ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī's al-ʿAwāmil al-miʾa, “the hundred governors”. Birgivī keeps the number a hundred but divides it differently, into governors, governed and iʿrāb, and gives each its chapter: the first on the governor, the second on the governed word, the third on iʿrāb.

The governor is of two kinds. Expressed (lafẓī): a word you hear, such as the particle bi- or the verb. Abstract (maʿnawī): no word at all, but an idea, such as a noun's being put at the head of a sentence. The expressed governor is again of two divisions. Heard (samāʿī): words known only from the usage of the Arabs, which must be learnt as a list, forty-nine in five kinds. Analogical (qiyāsī): a rule that covers whole classes of words, such as “every verb governs”, nine in all. With the two abstract governors that makes sixty.

Read the examples as you go. Nearly every sentence Birgivī gives teaches something besides grammar: tubtu min kulli dhanbin, “I have repented of every sin”; Muḥammadun rasūlu llāhi, “Muḥammad is the Messenger of God”. The child who learns the grammar learns the creed and the conduct with it, and the madrasa has always valued the book for both.

tasks.prompt: In tubtu min kulli dhanbin, name the governor, the governed word and the iʿrāb that min causes.
tasks.arabic: تُبْتُ مِنْ كُلِّ ذَنْبٍ
tasks.answer: The governor is min, a particle of jarr (heard). The governed word is kulli. The effect is jarr, shown by the kasra. (Dhanbin is in jarr too, but by iḍāfa: kullu governs it.)

tasks.prompt: Add up Birgivī's sixty governors by their kinds.
tasks.answer: Heard: 20 particles of jarr + 8 that give naṣb to the noun and rafʿ to the khabar + 2 that give rafʿ to the noun and naṣb to the khabar + 4 that put the present in naṣb + 15 that put it in jazm = 49. Analogical: 9. Abstract: 2. 49 + 9 + 2 = 60.

tasks.prompt: Expressed or abstract? (a) the governor of Muḥammadun in Muḥammadun rasūlu llāhi; (b) the governor of kulli in min kulli dhanbin.
tasks.arabic: مُحَمَّدٌ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ — مِنْ كُلِّ ذَنْبٍ
tasks.answer: (a) Abstract: no word stands before Muḥammad; its rafʿ comes from its being put first. (b) Expressed: the particle min.

tasks.prompt: What is the difference between a heard and an analogical governor? Give one of each.
tasks.answer: A heard governor is a word known from the Arabs' usage, learnt one by one from a list (for example the particle min). An analogical governor is a rule that covers a whole class of words (for example: every verb gives rafʿ and naṣb).

text.original: بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ. الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ، وَالصَّلَاةُ وَالسَّلَامُ عَلَى مُحَمَّدٍ وَآلِهِ أَجْمَعِينَ. وَبَعْدُ، فَاعْلَمْ أَنَّهُ لَا بُدَّ لِكُلِّ طَالِبِ مَعْرِفَةِ الْإِعْرَابِ مِنْ مَعْرِفَةِ مِائَةِ شَيْءٍ: سِتُّونَ مِنْهَا تُسَمَّى عَامِلًا، وَثَلَاثُونَ مِنْهَا تُسَمَّى مَعْمُولًا، وَعَشَرَةٌ مِنْهَا تُسَمَّى عَمَلًا وَإِعْرَابًا.
text.en: In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate. Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds, and blessing and peace upon Muḥammad and all his family. To proceed: know that everyone who seeks to know iʿrāb must know a hundred things: sixty of them are called governor (ʿāmil), thirty of them are called governed (maʿmūl), and ten of them are called the effect of governing (ʿamal) and iʿrāb.

text.original: فَأُبَيِّنُ لَكَ بِإِذْنِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى هَذِهِ الثَّلَاثَةَ عَلَى طَرِيقِ الْإِيجَازِ فِي ثَلَاثَةِ أَبْوَابٍ: الْبَابُ الْأَوَّلُ فِي الْعَامِلِ، الْبَابُ الثَّانِي فِي الْمَعْمُولِ، الْبَابُ الثَّالِثُ فِي الْإِعْرَابِ.
text.en: So I shall explain these three to you, by the leave of God Most High, by way of brevity, in three chapters: the first chapter on the governor, the second chapter on the governed word, and the third chapter on iʿrāb.

text.original: وَهُوَ عَلَى ضَرْبَيْنِ: لَفْظِيٌّ وَمَعْنَوِيٌّ. فَاللَّفْظِيُّ عَلَى قِسْمَيْنِ: سَمَاعِيٌّ وَقِيَاسِيٌّ. فَالسَّمَاعِيُّ تِسْعَةٌ وَأَرْبَعُونَ، وَأَنْوَاعُهُ خَمْسَةٌ.
text.en: It is of two kinds: expressed (lafẓī) and abstract (maʿnawī). The expressed is of two divisions: heard (samāʿī) and analogical (qiyāsī). The heard are forty-nine, and their kinds are five.

lessons.title: The particles of jarr (1)
body: The first kind of heard governor is the particles that put one noun in jarr, and only one: twenty of them, “called the particles of jarr and the particles of iḍāfa”. The second name says what they do in meaning: they join (aḍāfa) the meaning of a verb to a noun, as in tubtu ilā llāhi, where ilā joins “repenting” to God. Birgivī says jarr, the word of most books, where the Ājurrūmiyya says khafḍ.

The first ten, each with its example: bi-, “with, in”: āmantu bi-llāhi wa-bihi lā bi-ghayrihi, “I believe in God, in Him and not in another”; min, “from”: tubtu min kulli dhanbin; ilā, “to”: tubtu ilā llāhi taʿālā, “I have turned in repentance to God”; ʿan, “away from”: kafaftu ʿan al-ḥarāmi, “I have kept away from the forbidden”; ʿalā, “on, upon”: tajibu al-tawbatu ʿalā kulli mudhnibin, “repentance is a duty upon every sinner”.

Li-, “for, belonging to”: anā ʿubaydun li-llāhi taʿālā, “I am a little servant of God”, where ʿubayd is the diminutive of ʿabd that the Amthila taught. Fī, “in”: al-muṭīʿu fī al-jannati, “the obedient is in Paradise”. Ka-, “like”: laysa ka-mithlihi shayʾun, “there is nothing like Him” (Q 42:11); many grammarians take this ka- as added for emphasis, since “like” is already said by mithl. Ḥattā, “until”: aʿbudu llāha taʿālā ḥattā al-mawti, “I worship God until death”. Rubba, “many a”: rubba tālin yalʿanuhu al-qurʾānu, “many a reciter the Qurʾān curses”.

Two notes. Rubba comes only before an indefinite noun, here tālin, “a reciter”. Its yāʾ has dropped and the tanwīn stands on a kasra: the noun is in jarr, but the jarr is assumed on the lost yāʾ. And ḥattā has three faces in the madrasa books: a particle of jarr here, a particle of ʿaṭf in the Ājurrūmiyya (qadima al-ḥujjāju ḥattā al-mushātu), and a governor of the present verb (ḥattā takhruja). Before a noun in jarr, as in ḥattā al-mawti, it is the first.

tasks.prompt: Find each particle of jarr and the noun it governs: tubtu ilā llāhi taʿālā; al-muṭīʿu fī al-jannati; tajibu al-tawbatu ʿalā kulli mudhnibin.
tasks.arabic: تُبْتُ إِلَى اللَّهِ تَعَالَى — الْمُطِيعُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ — تَجِبُ التَّوْبَةُ عَلَى كُلِّ مُذْنِبٍ
tasks.answer: Ilā governs Allāhi; fī governs al-jannati; ʿalā governs kulli (and kulli governs mudhnibin by iḍāfa). Each noun after the particle is in jarr by the kasra.

tasks.prompt: What is ʿubayd in anā ʿubaydun li-llāhi, and what does it add to the meaning?
tasks.arabic: أَنَا عُبَيْدٌ لِلَّهِ تَعَالَى
tasks.answer: The diminutive of ʿabd on the pattern fuʿayl: “a little servant”. It expresses humility; the li- that follows puts Allāh in jarr.

tasks.prompt: Give the three uses of ḥattā in the books read so far, with an example of each, and say which one ḥattā al-mawti is.
tasks.answer: Particle of jarr: aʿbudu llāha ḥattā al-mawti (Birgivī). Particle of ʿaṭf: qadima al-ḥujjāju ḥattā al-mushātu (al-Ājurrūmiyya). Governor of naṣb of the present: ajlisu ḥattā takhruja. Ḥattā al-mawti is the first: al-mawti is in jarr.

tasks.prompt: In rubba tālin, why is there a kasra with tanwīn on the lām and no yāʾ?
tasks.arabic: رُبَّ تَالٍ
tasks.answer: Tālin, “a reciter”, is a noun whose last letter was a yāʾ (tālī). With tanwīn the yāʾ drops and the tanwīn stands on the kasra before it. It is in jarr by rubba, the jarr being assumed on the dropped yāʾ.

text.original: النَّوْعُ الْأَوَّلُ: حُرُوفٌ تَجُرُّ اسْمًا وَاحِدًا فَقَطْ، تُسَمَّى حُرُوفَ الْجَرِّ وَحُرُوفَ الْإِضَافَةِ، وَهِيَ عِشْرُونَ: الْأَوَّلُ الْبَاءُ، نَحْوُ: آمَنْتُ بِاللَّهِ وَبِهِ لَا بِغَيْرِهِ. وَالثَّانِي مِنْ، نَحْوُ: تُبْتُ مِنْ كُلِّ ذَنْبٍ. وَالثَّالِثُ إِلَى، نَحْوُ: تُبْتُ إِلَى اللَّهِ تَعَالَى. وَالرَّابِعُ عَنْ، نَحْوُ: كَفَفْتُ عَنِ الْحَرَامِ.
text.en: The first kind: particles that put one noun only in jarr; they are called the particles of jarr and the particles of iḍāfa, and they are twenty. The first is bi-, as āmantu bi-Allāhi wa-bihi lā bi-ghayrihi “I believe in God, and in Him, not in another”. The second is min, as tubtu min kulli dhanbin “I have repented of every sin”. The third is ilā, as tubtu ilā Allāhi taʿālā “I have turned in repentance to God Most High”. The fourth is ʿan, as kafaftu ʿani al-ḥarāmi “I have kept away from what is forbidden”.

text.original: وَالْخَامِسُ عَلَى، نَحْوُ: تَجِبُ التَّوْبَةُ عَلَى كُلِّ مُذْنِبٍ. وَالسَّادِسُ اللَّامُ، نَحْوُ: أَنَا عُبَيْدٌ لِلَّهِ تَعَالَى. وَالسَّابِعُ فِي، نَحْوُ: الْمُطِيعُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ. وَالثَّامِنُ الْكَافُ، نَحْوُ قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ. وَالتَّاسِعُ حَتَّى، نَحْوُ: أَعْبُدُ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى حَتَّى الْمَوْتِ. وَالْعَاشِرُ رُبَّ، نَحْوُ: رُبَّ تَالٍ يَلْعَنُهُ الْقُرْآنُ.
text.en: The fifth is ʿalā, as tajibu al-tawbatu ʿalā kulli mudhnibin “repentance is binding on every sinner”. The sixth is li-, as anā ʿubaydun li-Allāhi taʿālā “I am a little servant of God Most High”. The seventh is fī, as al-muṭīʿu fī al-jannati “the obedient one is in Paradise”. The eighth is ka-, as in His word, Most High: laysa ka-mithlihi shayʾun “there is nothing like Him”. The ninth is ḥattā, as aʿbudu Allāha taʿālā ḥattā al-mawti “I worship God Most High until death”. The tenth is rubba, as rubba tālin yalʿanuhu al-qurʾānu “many a reciter is cursed by the Qurʾān”.

lessons.title: The particles of jarr (2)
body: The second ten are a mixed company: two particles of the oath, three words of exception, two of time, and three that put a noun in jarr only in particular uses. Learnt together they complete the twenty.

The oath: wa-llāhi lā afʿalu al-kabāʾira, “By God, I do not commit the great sins”, with the wāw; ta-llāhi la-afʿalanna al-farāʾiḍa, “By God, I shall surely do the obligations”, with the tāʾ, which is used with the name of God only. In the second, la-afʿalanna is the answer of the oath, with a lām and a nūn of emphasis. The exception: halaka al-nāsu ḥāshā al-ʿālimi, “the people perish, except the scholar”; halaka al-ʿālimūna khalā al-ʿāmili bi-ʿamalihi, “the scholars perish, except the one who acts by his deeds”; halaka al-ʿāmilūna ʿadā al-mukhliṣi, “those who act perish, except the sincere”. The three run on like a chain, each step narrower than the one before. (An Ottoman lithograph reads bi-ʿilmihi, “by his knowledge”, in the second, which gives the better sense.)

Time: tubtu min kulli dhanbin faʿaltuhu mudh yawmi al-bulūghi, “I have repented of every sin I have done since the day I came of age”; tajibu al-ṣalātu mundhu yawmi al-bulūghi, “prayer is a duty from the day one comes of age”. Mudh and mundhu give the start of a time.

The last three put a noun in jarr only in special cases. Lawlā with an attached pronoun: lawlāka yā raḥmata llāhi la-halaka al-nāsu, “were it not for you, O mercy of God, the people would have perished”; Sībawayh held that lawlā is then a particle of jarr, while others say the pronoun stands in the place of rafʿ. Kay before the mā of the question, shortened to kaymah: kaymah ʿaṣayta, “why did you disobey?”. And laʿalla in the dialect of the tribe of ʿUqayl, who said laʿalla llāhi taʿālā yaghfiru dhanbī, “perhaps God will forgive my sin”, with jarr; in the common language laʿalla is a sister of inna (next lesson).

So the same word can govern in different ways: ḥāshā, khalā and ʿadā put a noun in jarr here, but the Ājurrūmiyya allowed naṣb after them too; laʿalla puts its noun in jarr in one dialect and in naṣb in all the others. Birgivī counts a word among the particles of jarr wherever it gives jarr.

tasks.arabic: هَلَكَ الْعَامِلُونَ عَدَا الْمُخْلِصِ — وَاللَّهِ لَا أَفْعَلُ الْكَبَائِرَ — مُذْ يَوْمِ الْبُلُوغِ
tasks.answer: ʿAdā governs al-mukhliṣi; the wāw of the oath governs Allāhi; mudh governs yawmi (and yawmi governs al-bulūghi by iḍāfa).

tasks.prompt: Read the three sentences with ḥāshā, khalā and ʿadā in order and explain how they form a chain.
tasks.answer: The people perish except the scholar; the scholars perish except the one who acts by what he knows; those who act perish except the sincere. Each sentence takes the exception of the one before as its new subject, narrowing it each time.

tasks.prompt: What is kaymah, and what does kaymah ʿaṣayta mean?
tasks.arabic: كَيْمَهْ عَصَيْتَ
tasks.answer: Kay, a particle of jarr here, with the mā of the question shortened to ma and a hāʾ of pause: “for what?”, “why?”. Kaymah ʿaṣayta: “why did you disobey?”.

tasks.prompt: Why does laʿalla llāhi have a kasra on the name of God, when the next lesson has laʿalla llāha?
tasks.answer: In the dialect of the tribe of ʿUqayl, laʿalla is a particle of jarr and puts the noun after it in jarr. In the common language it is a sister of inna and puts its noun in naṣb: laʿalla llāha taʿālā ghāfirun dhanbī.

quiz.prompt: The tāʾ of the oath is used with…
quiz.explanation: Ta-llāhi; with other nouns the wāw or the bāʾ is used.

quiz.prompt: In halaka al-nāsu ḥāshā al-ʿālimi, ḥāshā is…
options: a particle of jarr used for exception
quiz.explanation: Al-ʿālimi is in jarr by it.

quiz.prompt: What do mudh and mundhu give?
options: The end of a time: until
The start of a time: since
quiz.explanation: Mudh yawmi al-bulūghi: since the day of coming of age.

quiz.prompt: In the dialect of ʿUqayl, laʿalla…
quiz.explanation: Laʿalla llāhi taʿālā yaghfiru dhanbī.

quiz.prompt: What did Sībawayh hold about lawlā with a pronoun (lawlāka)?
options: That the pronoun is in naṣb
That lawlā is then a particle of jarr
quiz.explanation: Others say the pronoun stands in the place of rafʿ.

quiz.prompt: What does kaymah ʿaṣayta mean?
quiz.explanation: Kay with the mā of the question: “for what?”.

quiz.prompt: In ta-llāhi la-afʿalanna al-farāʾiḍa, la-afʿalanna is…
quiz.explanation: The oath is answered with a lām and a nūn of emphasis.

text.original: وَالْحَادِي عَشَرَ وَاوُ الْقَسَمِ، نَحْوُ: وَاللَّهِ لَا أَفْعَلُ الْكَبَائِرَ. وَالثَّانِي عَشَرَ تَاءُ الْقَسَمِ، نَحْوُ: تَاللَّهِ لَأَفْعَلَنَّ الْفَرَائِضَ. وَالثَّالِثَ عَشَرَ حَاشَا، نَحْوُ: هَلَكَ النَّاسُ حَاشَا الْعَالِمِ. وَالرَّابِعَ عَشَرَ مُذْ، نَحْوُ: تُبْتُ مِنْ كُلِّ ذَنْبٍ فَعَلْتُهُ مُذْ يَوْمِ الْبُلُوغِ. وَالْخَامِسَ عَشَرَ مُنْذُ، نَحْوُ: تَجِبُ الصَّلَاةُ مُنْذُ يَوْمِ الْبُلُوغِ.
text.en: The eleventh is the wāw of oath, as wa-Allāhi lā afʿalu al-kabāʾira “by God, I do not commit the great sins”. The twelfth is the tāʾ of oath, as ta-Allāhi la-afʿalanna al-farāʾiḍa “by God, I shall surely do the obligations”. The thirteenth is ḥāshā, as halaka al-nāsu ḥāshā al-ʿālimi “the people perished, save the scholar”. The fourteenth is mudh, as tubtu min kulli dhanbin faʿaltuhu mudh yawmi al-bulūghi “I have repented of every sin I have done since the day I came of age”. The fifteenth is mundhu, as tajibu al-ṣalātu mundhu yawmi al-bulūghi “prayer is binding from the day of coming of age”.

text.original: وَالسَّادِسَ عَشَرَ خَلَا، نَحْوُ: هَلَكَ الْعَالِمُونَ خَلَا الْعَامِلِ بِعَمَلِهِ. وَالسَّابِعَ عَشَرَ عَدَا، نَحْوُ: هَلَكَ الْعَامِلُونَ عَدَا الْمُخْلِصِ. وَالثَّامِنَ عَشَرَ لَوْلَا، نَحْوُ: لَوْلَاكَ يَا رَحْمَةَ اللَّهِ لَهَلَكَ النَّاسُ. وَالتَّاسِعَ عَشَرَ كَيْ، نَحْوُ: كَيْمَهْ عَصَيْتَ. وَالْعِشْرُونَ لَعَلَّ فِي لُغَةِ عُقَيْلٍ، نَحْوُ: لَعَلَّ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى يَغْفِرُ ذَنْبِي.
text.en: The sixteenth is khalā, as halaka al-ʿālimūna khalā al-ʿāmili bi-ʿamalihi “the scholars perished, save the one who acts in his deeds”. The seventeenth is ʿadā, as halaka al-ʿāmilūna ʿadā al-mukhliṣi “those who act perished, except the sincere”. The eighteenth is lawlā, as lawlāka yā raḥmata Allāhi la-halaka al-nāsu “were it not for you, O mercy of God, the people would have perished”. The nineteenth is kay, as kaymah ʿaṣayta “for what did you disobey?”. The twentieth is laʿalla in the dialect of ʿUqayl, as laʿalla Allāhi taʿālā yaghfiru dhanbī “perhaps God Most High will forgive my sin”.

lessons.title: Inna and its sisters, illā and lā
body: The second kind of heard governor is eight particles that put the noun in naṣb and the khabar in rafʿ. Six are those of the Ājurrūmiyya, “called the particles like the verb”: inna, anna, kaʾanna, lākinna, layta, laʿalla. Birgivī adds two more that do the same work: illā in the cut-off exception, and lā that denies the whole kind. His list is drawn by what a word does, not by what it means.

His examples teach the creed. Inna llāha taʿālā ʿālimu kulli shayʾin, “God Most High is the knower of everything”; aʿtaqidu anna llāha taʿālā qādirun ʿalā kulli shayʾin, “I hold that God Most High has power over everything”, where anna stands inside the sentence as the object of aʿtaqidu. Kaʾanna al-ḥarāma nārun, “it is as if the forbidden were fire”. Mā fāza al-jāhilu lākinna al-ʿālima fāʾizun, “the ignorant does not succeed, but the scholar succeeds”. Layta al-ʿilma marzūqun li-kulli aḥadin, “if only knowledge were granted to everyone”. Laʿalla llāha taʿālā ghāfirun dhanbī, “perhaps God Most High forgives my sin”.

Illā in the cut-off exception (al-istithnāʾ al-munqaṭiʿ), where what is excepted is not of the kind of what came before: al-maʿṣiyatu mubʿidatun ʿan al-jannati illā al-ṭāʿata muqarribatun minhā, “sin takes one far from Paradise, but obedience brings one near it”. Obedience is not a kind of sin, so it is not taken out of it; illā here means “but”, and Birgivī counts it with lākinna: al-ṭāʿata its noun in naṣb, muqarribatun its khabar in rafʿ.

Lā that denies the whole kind: lā fāʿila sharrin fāʾizun, “no doer of evil succeeds”. Its noun fāʿila sharrin is joined to the word after it, so it shows a plain fatḥa (the single noun of the Ājurrūmiyya, lā rajula, had a fixed ending without tanwīn); its khabar fāʾizun is in rafʿ.

In the iʿrāb the madrasa names each part: inna, a particle like the verb, of emphasis; llāha, its noun, in naṣb; ʿālimu, its khabar, in rafʿ, and the first term of an iḍāfa; kulli, in jarr as the second term; shayʾin, in jarr as the second term of a second iḍāfa.

terms.en: the six particles like the verb
the cut-off exception: the excepted is of another kind
the lā that denies the whole kind
the noun of inna (naṣb) and its khabar (rafʿ)

tasks.prompt: Give the noun and the khabar of each particle, with their states: kaʾanna al-ḥarāma nārun; layta al-ʿilma marzūqun li-kulli aḥadin; lā fāʿila sharrin fāʾizun.
tasks.arabic: كَأَنَّ الْحَرَامَ نَارٌ — لَيْتَ الْعِلْمَ مَرْزُوقٌ لِكُلِّ أَحَدٍ — لَا فَاعِلَ شَرٍّ فَائِزٌ
tasks.answer: Kaʾanna: noun al-ḥarāma (naṣb), khabar nārun (rafʿ). Layta: noun al-ʿilma (naṣb), khabar marzūqun (rafʿ). Lā: noun fāʿila (naṣb, joined to sharrin), khabar fāʾizun (rafʿ).

tasks.prompt: Why does Birgivī count illā among these governors in al-maʿṣiyatu mubʿidatun ʿan al-jannati illā al-ṭāʿata muqarribatun minhā?
tasks.arabic: إِلَّا الطَّاعَةَ مُقَرِّبَةٌ مِنْهَا
tasks.answer: The exception is cut off: obedience is not a kind of sin, so nothing is taken out of the first statement. Illā then means “but”, like lākinna, and works like it: al-ṭāʿata is its noun in naṣb and muqarribatun its khabar in rafʿ.

tasks.prompt: Give the full iʿrāb of inna llāha taʿālā ʿālimu kulli shayʾin.
tasks.arabic: إِنَّ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى عَالِمُ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ
tasks.answer: Inna: a particle like the verb, of emphasis. Llāha: its noun, in naṣb by the fatḥa. Taʿālā: a verb with its hidden doer, a sentence of praise set between (“exalted is He”). ʿĀlimu: the khabar of inna, in rafʿ by the ḍamma, and the first term of an iḍāfa. Kulli: in jarr as the second term, and itself the first term of another. Shayʾin: in jarr as the second term.

tasks.prompt: How does Birgivī's list of these governors differ from the Ājurrūmiyya's sisters of inna?
tasks.answer: The Ājurrūmiyya gives the six particles like the verb. Birgivī adds illā in the cut-off exception and the lā that denies the kind, because they do the same work: naṣb of the noun, rafʿ of the khabar.

quiz.prompt: What do the eight particles of this kind do?
options: Naṣb of the noun, rafʿ of the khabar
Rafʿ of the noun, naṣb of the khabar
quiz.explanation: Inna llāha … ʿālimu.

quiz.prompt: Which two does Birgivī add to the six of the Ājurrūmiyya?
options: Illā in the cut-off exception and the lā of the kind
quiz.explanation: They do the same work as inna.

quiz.prompt: What is a cut-off (munqaṭiʿ) exception?
options: One where the excepted is not of the kind of what came before
quiz.explanation: Obedience is not a kind of sin.

quiz.prompt: In lā fāʿila sharrin fāʾizun, why does fāʿila show a plain fatḥa?
options: It is joined to the next word (muḍāf)
quiz.explanation: A single noun after lā has a fixed ending; a muḍāf noun is in naṣb.

quiz.prompt: In aʿtaqidu anna llāha taʿālā qādirun, the clause with anna is…
quiz.explanation: Anna stands inside the sentence, its clause in the place of a noun.

quiz.prompt: Which particle means “if only”?
quiz.explanation: Layta al-ʿilma marzūqun li-kulli aḥadin.

quiz.prompt: By what does Birgivī group his governors?
options: By what they do to the words they govern
quiz.explanation: So illā and lā stand beside inna.

text.original: النَّوْعُ الثَّانِي: حُرُوفٌ تَنْصِبُ الِاسْمَ وَتَرْفَعُ الْخَبَرَ، وَهِيَ ثَمَانِيَةٌ: الْأَوَّلُ إِنَّ، نَحْوُ: إِنَّ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى عَالِمُ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ. وَالثَّانِي أَنَّ، نَحْوُ: أَعْتَقِدُ أَنَّ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى قَادِرٌ عَلَى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ. وَالثَّالِثُ كَأَنَّ، نَحْوُ: كَأَنَّ الْحَرَامَ نَارٌ. وَالرَّابِعُ لَكِنَّ، نَحْوُ: مَا فَازَ الْجَاهِلُ لَكِنَّ الْعَالِمَ فَائِزٌ.
text.en: The second kind: particles that put the noun in naṣb and the khabar in rafʿ; they are eight. The first is inna, as inna Allāha taʿālā ʿālimu kulli shayʾin “indeed God Most High is the knower of everything”. The second is anna, as aʿtaqidu anna Allāha taʿālā qādirun ʿalā kulli shayʾin “I believe that God Most High has power over everything”. The third is kaʾanna, as kaʾanna al-ḥarāma nārun “it is as if the forbidden were fire”. The fourth is lākinna, as mā fāza al-jāhilu lākinna al-ʿālima fāʾizun “the ignorant did not succeed, but the scholar is successful”.

text.original: وَالْخَامِسُ لَيْتَ، نَحْوُ: لَيْتَ الْعِلْمَ مَرْزُوقٌ لِكُلِّ أَحَدٍ. وَالسَّادِسُ لَعَلَّ، نَحْوُ: لَعَلَّ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى غَافِرٌ ذَنْبِي. وَهَذِهِ السِّتَّةُ تُسَمَّى الْحُرُوفَ الْمُشَبَّهَةَ بِالْفِعْلِ. وَالسَّابِعُ إِلَّا فِي الِاسْتِثْنَاءِ الْمُنْقَطِعِ، نَحْوُ: الْمَعْصِيَةُ مُبْعِدَةٌ عَنِ الْجَنَّةِ إِلَّا الطَّاعَةَ مُقَرِّبَةٌ مِنْهَا. وَالثَّامِنُ لَا لِنَفْيِ الْجِنْسِ، نَحْوُ: لَا فَاعِلَ شَرٍّ فَائِزٌ.
text.en: The fifth is layta, as layta al-ʿilma marzūqun li-kulli aḥadin “if only knowledge were granted to everyone”. The sixth is laʿalla, as laʿalla Allāha taʿālā ghāfirun dhanbī “perhaps God Most High forgives my sin”. These six are called the particles that resemble the verb. The seventh is illā in the disconnected exception (al-istithnāʾ al-munqaṭiʿ), as al-maʿṣiyatu mubʿidatun ʿani al-jannati illā al-ṭāʿata muqarribatun minhā “disobedience takes one far from Paradise, but obedience brings one near to it”. The eighth is the lā that denies the whole kind, as lā fāʿila sharrin fāʾizun “no doer of evil is successful”.

lessons.title: Mā and lā like laysa; the four governors of naṣb
body: The third kind is two particles that do the opposite of inna: they put the noun in rafʿ and the khabar in naṣb, like laysa, “is not”. They are mā and lā “resembling laysa”: mā llāhu taʿālā mutamakkinan bi-makānin, “God Most High is not settled in a place”; lā shayʾun mushābihan li-llāhi taʿālā, “nothing is like God Most High”. Both sentences are points of the creed: God is not in a place, and nothing resembles Him.

Mā used in this way is the usage of the people of the Ḥijāz, the language of the Qurʾān, and the grammarians call it mā al-ḥijāziyya; the tribe of Tamīm let mā govern nothing. Lā works like laysa with an indefinite noun, as shayʾun here. Set this beside the last lesson and the same lā appears with opposite effects: lā fāʿila sharrin fāʾizun, noun in naṣb and khabar in rafʿ (the lā of the kind); lā shayʾun mushābihan, noun in rafʿ and khabar in naṣb (the lā like laysa). The endings tell you which lā you have.

The fourth kind is four particles that put the present verb in naṣb: an: uḥibbu an uṭīʿa llāha taʿālā, “I love to obey God Most High”; lan: lan yaghfira llāhu taʿālā li-l-kāfirīna, “God will never forgive the unbelievers”; kay: uḥibbu ṭūla al-ʿumuri kay uḥaṣṣila al-ʿilma, “I love a long life so that I may gain knowledge”; idhan: idhan tadkhula al-jannata, “then you will enter Paradise”, said to one who says “I obey God”.

The Ājurrūmiyya counted ten governors of naṣb; Birgivī counts four. He follows the Baṣran view that the lām of kay, the lām of denial, ḥattā and the fāʾ, wāw and aw of the answer put the verb in naṣb through an an that is understood, so they are not governors in their own right. The madrasa student who reads both books learns the two counts and why they differ.

terms.en: mā and lā like laysa: rafʿ of the noun, naṣb of the khabar
the mā of the Ḥijāz, which works like laysa
the governors of naṣb of the present: an, lan, kay, idhan
the an that is understood, on the Baṣran view

examples.en: mā llāhu taʿālā mutamakkinan bi-makānin, “God Most High is not settled in a place”
lā shayʾun mushābihan li-llāhi taʿālā, “nothing is like God Most High”
uḥibbu an uṭīʿa llāha taʿālā, “I love to obey God Most High”: an with the verb in naṣb
idhan tadkhula al-jannata, “then you will enter Paradise”: idhan answering what was said

tasks.prompt: Give the noun and the khabar, with their states: mā llāhu taʿālā mutamakkinan bi-makānin; lā shayʾun mushābihan li-llāhi taʿālā.
tasks.arabic: مَا اللَّهُ تَعَالَى مُتَمَكِّنًا بِمَكَانٍ — لَا شَيْءٌ مُشَابِهًا لِلَّهِ تَعَالَى
tasks.answer: Mā: noun llāhu (rafʿ), khabar mutamakkinan (naṣb). Lā: noun shayʾun (rafʿ), khabar mushābihan (naṣb).

tasks.prompt: Lā fāʿila sharrin fāʾizun and lā shayʾun mushābihan: which lā is each, and how do the endings show it?
tasks.arabic: لَا فَاعِلَ شَرٍّ فَائِزٌ — لَا شَيْءٌ مُشَابِهًا
tasks.answer: The first is the lā of the whole kind: its noun is in naṣb (fāʿila) and its khabar in rafʿ (fāʾizun). The second is the lā like laysa: its noun is in rafʿ (shayʾun) and its khabar in naṣb (mushābihan).

tasks.prompt: Find the governor of naṣb and the verb it governs: lan yaghfira llāhu taʿālā li-l-kāfirīna; uḥibbu ṭūla al-ʿumuri kay uḥaṣṣila al-ʿilma.
tasks.arabic: لَنْ يَغْفِرَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى لِلْكَافِرِينَ — أُحِبُّ طُولَ الْعُمُرِ كَيْ أُحَصِّلَ الْعِلْمَ
tasks.answer: Lan governs yaghfira, in naṣb by the fatḥa. Kay governs uḥaṣṣila, in naṣb by the fatḥa.

tasks.prompt: Why does Birgivī count four governors of naṣb where the Ājurrūmiyya counts ten?
tasks.answer: He follows the Baṣran view: only an, lan, kay and idhan govern by themselves. After the lām of kay, the lām of denial, ḥattā and the fāʾ, wāw and aw of the answer, the verb is in naṣb by an understood an.

Rafʿ of the noun, naṣb of the khabar

quiz.explanation: Hence its name, mā al-ḥijāziyya.

quiz.prompt: In lā shayʾun mushābihan li-llāhi, mushābihan is…
options: the noun of lā, in naṣb
the khabar of lā, in naṣb
quiz.explanation: Lā like laysa puts the khabar in naṣb.

quiz.prompt: How many governors of naṣb of the present does Birgivī count?
quiz.explanation: An, lan, kay, idhan.

quiz.prompt: Idhan tadkhula al-jannata is said…
options: at the start of a speech
in answer to someone who says “I obey God”
quiz.explanation: Idhan answers what was said: “then you will enter Paradise”.

quiz.prompt: Which is the lā like laysa?
quiz.explanation: Noun in rafʿ, khabar in naṣb.

quiz.prompt: On the Baṣran view, after ḥattā the verb is in naṣb by…
quiz.explanation: So Birgivī does not count ḥattā among the governors of naṣb.

text.original: النَّوْعُ الثَّالِثُ: حَرْفَانِ يَرْفَعَانِ الِاسْمَ وَيَنْصِبَانِ الْخَبَرَ، وَهُمَا مَا وَلَا الْمُشَبَّهَتَانِ بِلَيْسَ، نَحْوُ: مَا اللَّهُ تَعَالَى مُتَمَكِّنًا بِمَكَانٍ، وَلَا شَيْءٌ مُشَابِهًا لِلَّهِ تَعَالَى.
text.en: The third kind: two particles that put the noun in rafʿ and the khabar in naṣb; they are mā and lā that resemble laysa, as mā Allāhu taʿālā mutamakkinan bi-makānin “God Most High is not settled in a place” and wa-lā shayʾun mushābihan li-Allāhi taʿālā “and nothing is like God Most High”.

text.original: النَّوْعُ الرَّابِعُ: حُرُوفٌ تَنْصِبُ الْفِعْلَ الْمُضَارِعَ، وَهِيَ أَرْبَعَةٌ: الْأَوَّلُ أَنْ، نَحْوُ: أُحِبُّ أَنْ أُطِيعَ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى. وَالثَّانِي لَنْ، نَحْوُ: لَنْ يَغْفِرَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى لِلْكَافِرِينَ. وَالثَّالِثُ كَيْ، نَحْوُ: أُحِبُّ طُولَ الْعُمُرِ كَيْ أُحَصِّلَ الْعِلْمَ. وَالرَّابِعُ إِذَنْ، نَحْوُ قَوْلِكَ: إِذَنْ تَدْخُلَ الْجَنَّةَ، لِمَنْ قَالَ: أُطِيعُ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى.
text.en: The fourth kind: particles that put the muḍāriʿ verb in naṣb; they are four. The first is an, as uḥibbu an uṭīʿa Allāha taʿālā “I love to obey God Most High”. The second is lan, as lan yaghfira Allāhu taʿālā li-al-kāfirīna “God Most High will never forgive the unbelievers”. The third is kay, as uḥibbu ṭūla al-ʿumuri kay uḥaṣṣila al-ʿilma “I love a long life, so that I may gain knowledge”. The fourth is idhan, as when you say idhan tadkhula al-jannata “then you will enter Paradise” to one who says uṭīʿu Allāha taʿālā “I obey God Most High”.

lessons.title: The fifteen governors of jazm
body: The fifth kind of heard governor is fifteen words that put the present verb in jazm. Four govern one verb only: lam: lam yalid wa-lam yūlad, “He did not beget and was not begotten” (Q 112:3); lammā: lammā yanfaʿ ʿumurī, “my life has not yet been of use”; the lām of command: li-yaʿmal ʿamalan ṣāliḥan, “let him do a good deed”; and the lā of prohibition: lā tudhnib, “do not sin”.

Eleven govern two verbs, “called condition and requital” (sharṭ and jazāʾ): in, mahmā, mā, man, ayna, matā, annā, ayy, ḥaythumā, idhmā and idhā mā. In tatub tughfar dhunūbuka, “if you repent, your sins will be forgiven”: tatub is the condition, tughfar the requital, both in jazm. Man yaʿmal ʿamalan ṣāliḥan yakun nājiyan, “whoever does a good deed will be saved”. Ayna takun yudrikka al-mawtu, “wherever you are, death will overtake you”. Matā taḥsud tahlik, “whenever you envy, you perish”.

Each word of condition adds its meaning: in “if”, man “whoever”, mā and mahmā “whatever”, ayna, annā and ḥaythumā “wherever”, matā “whenever”, ayy “whichever”: ayyu ʿālimin yatakabbar yubghiḍhu llāhu taʿālā, “whichever scholar is proud, God hates him”. Idhmā and idhā mā mean “whenever, if”: idhā mā taʿmal bi-ʿilmika takun khayra al-nāsi, “if you act by your knowledge, you will be the best of people”.

Compare the eighteen of the Ājurrūmiyya. Birgivī leaves out alam and alammā, which are lam and lammā with the hamza of the question, kayfamā, which the Baṣrans do not count, and ayyāna; and where the Ājurrūmiyya has idhā in poetry, he has idhā mā. The same rule stands behind both lists: one verb in jazm after the first four, two after the words of condition.

Look at the verbs in jazm: several are weak. Tatub from tatūbu and takun from takūnu lose the long vowel before the sukūn; lam yalid has lost the wāw of its root already in the present. The ṣarf books, the Binā and the Maqṣūd, explain these changes; here it is enough that the sign of jazm is the sukūn on the last letter.

terms.en: the governors of jazm: fifteen in this book
the condition: the first verb
the requital: the second verb, the answer
the words of condition: in, man, mā …

examples.en: lam yalid wa-lam yūlad, “He did not beget and was not begotten” (Q 112:3): lam, one verb
lā tudhnib, “do not sin”: the lā of prohibition
in tatub tughfar dhunūbuka, “if you repent, your sins will be forgiven”: condition and requital

examples.arabic: مَنْ يَعْمَلْ عَمَلًا صَالِحًا يَكُنْ نَاجِيًا
examples.en: man yaʿmal ʿamalan ṣāliḥan yakun nājiyan, “whoever does a good deed will be saved”

tasks.prompt: Name the condition and the requital, and the sign of jazm of each: man yaʿmal ʿamalan ṣāliḥan yakun nājiyan; matā taḥsud tahlik.
tasks.arabic: مَنْ يَعْمَلْ عَمَلًا صَالِحًا يَكُنْ نَاجِيًا — مَتَى تَحْسُدْ تَهْلِكْ
tasks.answer: Man: condition yaʿmal, requital yakun; both in jazm by the sukūn (yakun has lost its long ū before the sukūn). Matā: condition taḥsud, requital tahlik; both in jazm by the sukūn.

tasks.prompt: Which four of the fifteen put only one verb in jazm? Give Birgivī's example of each.
tasks.answer: Lam (lam yalid wa-lam yūlad), lammā (lammā yanfaʿ ʿumurī), the lām of command (li-yaʿmal ʿamalan ṣāliḥan) and the lā of prohibition (lā tudhnib).

tasks.prompt: In in tatub tughfar dhunūbuka, what is dhunūbuka, and why is tughfar passive?
tasks.arabic: إِنْ تَتُبْ تُغْفَرْ ذُنُوبُكَ
tasks.answer: Tughfar is the passive present in jazm (the requital): “will be forgiven”. Dhunūbuka is its deputy of the doer (nāʾib al-fāʿil), in rafʿ: “your sins”. The one who forgives is not named.

tasks.prompt: Which governors of jazm of the Ājurrūmiyya does Birgivī leave out, and what does he have instead of idhā?
tasks.answer: He leaves out alam and alammā (lam and lammā with the hamza of the question), kayfamā and ayyāna. Instead of idhā (in poetry only) he has idhā mā.

quiz.prompt: How many governors of jazm does Birgivī count?
quiz.explanation: Four of one verb and eleven of two.

quiz.prompt: Which governs two verbs?
quiz.explanation: The words of condition govern the condition and the requital.

quiz.prompt: What does Birgivī call the two verbs after a word of condition?
quiz.explanation: The second is the answer, which he calls requital.

quiz.prompt: In ayna takun yudrikka al-mawtu, al-mawtu is…
options: the doer of yudrik, in rafʿ
quiz.explanation: Death overtakes you: al-mawtu is the doer; -ka is the object.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is not in Birgivī's list?
quiz.explanation: The Baṣrans do not count kayfamā; the Ājurrūmiyya follows the Kūfans.

quiz.prompt: Matā taḥsud tahlik means…
quiz.explanation: Matā: “whenever”.

quiz.prompt: What is the sign of jazm in lā tudhnib?
options: The dropping of a weak letter
quiz.explanation: Tudhnibu → lā tudhnib.

text.original: النَّوْعُ الْخَامِسُ: كَلِمَاتٌ تَجْزِمُ الْفِعْلَ الْمُضَارِعَ، وَهِيَ خَمْسَ عَشْرَةَ: الْأُولَى لَمْ، نَحْوُ قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: لَمْ يَلِدْ وَلَمْ يُولَدْ. وَالثَّانِيَةُ لَمَّا، نَحْوُ: لَمَّا يَنْفَعْ عُمُرِي. وَالثَّالِثَةُ لَامُ الْأَمْرِ، نَحْوُ: لِيَعْمَلْ عَمَلًا صَالِحًا. وَالرَّابِعَةُ لَا فِي النَّهْيِ، نَحْوُ: لَا تُذْنِبْ. وَهَذِهِ الْأَرْبَعَةُ تَجْزِمُ فِعْلًا وَاحِدًا.
text.en: The fifth kind: words that put the muḍāriʿ verb in jazm; they are fifteen. The first is lam, as in His word, Most High: lam yalid wa-lam yūlad “He did not beget, and was not begotten”. The second is lammā, as lammā yanfaʿ ʿumurī “my life has not yet been of use”. The third is the lām of command, as li-yaʿmal ʿamalan ṣāliḥan “let him do a righteous deed”. The fourth is lā in prohibition, as lā tudhnib “do not sin”. These four put one verb in jazm.

text.original: وَالْخَامِسَةُ إِنْ، نَحْوُ: إِنْ تَتُبْ تُغْفَرْ ذُنُوبُكَ. وَالسَّادِسَةُ مَهْمَا، نَحْوُ: مَهْمَا تَفْعَلْ تُسْأَلْ عَنْهُ. وَالسَّابِعَةُ مَا، نَحْوُ: مَا تَفْعَلْ مِنْ خَيْرٍ تَجِدْهُ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى. وَالثَّامِنَةُ مَنْ، نَحْوُ: مَنْ يَعْمَلْ عَمَلًا صَالِحًا يَكُنْ نَاجِيًا. وَالتَّاسِعَةُ أَيْنَ، نَحْوُ: أَيْنَ تَكُنْ يُدْرِكْكَ الْمَوْتُ. وَالْعَاشِرَةُ مَتَى، نَحْوُ: مَتَى تَحْسُدْ تَهْلِكْ.
text.en: The fifth is in, as in tatub tughfar dhunūbuka “if you repent, your sins will be forgiven”. The sixth is mahmā, as mahmā tafʿal tusʾal ʿanhu “whatever you do, you will be asked about it”. The seventh is mā, as mā tafʿal min khayrin tajidhu ʿinda Allāhi taʿālā “whatever good you do, you will find it with God Most High”. The eighth is man, as man yaʿmal ʿamalan ṣāliḥan yakun nājiyan “whoever does a righteous deed will be saved”. The ninth is ayna, as ayna takun yudrikka al-mawtu “wherever you are, death will overtake you”. The tenth is matā, as matā taḥsud tahlik “whenever you envy, you perish”.

text.original: وَالْحَادِيَةَ عَشْرَةَ أَنَّى، نَحْوُ: أَنَّى تُذْنِبْ يَعْلَمْكَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى. وَالثَّانِيَةَ عَشْرَةَ أَيٌّ، نَحْوُ: أَيُّ عَالِمٍ يَتَكَبَّرْ يُبْغِضْهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى. وَالثَّالِثَةَ عَشْرَةَ حَيْثُمَا، نَحْوُ: حَيْثُمَا تَفْعَلْ يُكْتَبْ فِعْلُكَ. وَالرَّابِعَةَ عَشْرَةَ إِذْمَا، نَحْوُ: إِذْمَا تَتُبْ تُقْبَلْ تَوْبَتُكَ. وَالْخَامِسَةَ عَشْرَةَ إِذَا مَا، نَحْوُ: إِذَا مَا تَعْمَلْ بِعِلْمِكَ تَكُنْ خَيْرَ النَّاسِ. وَهَذِهِ الْإِحْدَى عَشْرَةَ تَجْزِمُ فِعْلَيْنِ مُسَمَّيَيْنِ شَرْطًا وَجَزَاءً.
text.en: The eleventh is annā, as annā tudhnib yaʿlamka Allāhu taʿālā “wherever you sin, God Most High knows of you”. The twelfth is ayy, as ayyu ʿālimin yatakabbar yubghiḍhu Allāhu taʿālā “whichever scholar is proud, God Most High hates him”. The thirteenth is ḥaythumā, as ḥaythumā tafʿal yuktab fiʿluka “wherever you act, your act is written down”. The fourteenth is idhmā, as idhmā tatub tuqbal tawbatuka “if you repent, your repentance is accepted”. The fifteenth is idhā mā, as idhā mā taʿmal bi-ʿilmika takun khayra al-nāsi “when you act on your knowledge, you are the best of people”. These eleven put two verbs in jazm, which are called the condition (sharṭ) and the answer (jazāʾ).

lessons.title: The verb as governor: complete and incomplete
body: Now the analogical governors, nine rules that each cover a whole class of words. The first and greatest is the verb: “every verb gives rafʿ and naṣb”. In khalaqa llāhu taʿālā kulla shayʾin, “God Most High created everything”, the verb gives rafʿ to its doer and naṣb to its object. And even a verb without an object gives naṣb to something: nazala al-qurʾānu nuzūlan, “the Qurʾān came down, a coming down”, where nuzūlan is an absolute object. A verb may lack an object, but never the power to put something in naṣb: its maṣdar, a time, a place, a state.

“Every verb must have a noun in rafʿ.” If the statement is complete with that noun, the verb is complete (tāmm): ʿalima llāhu taʿālā, “God Most High knew”. If it is not, but needs a khabar in naṣb as well, the verb is incomplete (nāqiṣ): kāna llāhu taʿālā ʿalīman ḥakīman, “God Most High is All-Knowing, All-Wise”.

The incomplete verbs are the sisters of kāna of the Ājurrūmiyya, and Birgivī gives several of them with sentences of the creed and of fiqh: ṣāra al-ʿāṣī mustaḥiqqan li-l-ʿadhābi, “the disobedient has become deserving of punishment”; mā zāla al-mudhnibu baʿīdan min allāhi taʿālā, “the sinner is still far from God”; tuqbalu al-tawbatu mā dāma al-rūḥu dākhilan fī al-badani, “repentance is accepted as long as the soul is within the body”; laysa llāhu taʿālā jisman, “God Most High is not a body”.

So where the Ājurrūmiyya treated kāna among the words that enter the subject and predicate, Birgivī treats it as a verb, governed by the same rule as every verb, and the difference between complete and incomplete is only whether the noun in rafʿ is enough. In kāna llāhu ʿalīman the noun in rafʿ is llāhu, the noun of kāna, and ʿalīman its khabar in naṣb.

terms.en: the complete verb: its noun in rafʿ completes it
the incomplete verb: it needs a khabar in naṣb
the analogical governor: a rule for a class of words
the absolute object: nuzūlan in nazala … nuzūlan

examples.en: khalaqa llāhu taʿālā kulla shayʾin, “God Most High created everything”: rafʿ of the doer, naṣb of the object
nazala al-qurʾānu nuzūlan, “the Qurʾān came down”: a verb without an object still gives naṣb
kāna llāhu taʿālā ʿalīman ḥakīman: an incomplete verb with its noun and khabar
laysa llāhu taʿālā jisman, “God Most High is not a body”

tasks.prompt: What does the verb give rafʿ and naṣb to in khalaqa llāhu taʿālā kulla shayʾin and in nazala al-qurʾānu nuzūlan?
tasks.arabic: خَلَقَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى كُلَّ شَيْءٍ — نَزَلَ الْقُرْآنُ نُزُولًا
tasks.answer: Khalaqa: rafʿ to llāhu (its doer), naṣb to kulla (its object). Nazala: rafʿ to al-qurʾānu (its doer), naṣb to nuzūlan (its absolute object).

tasks.prompt: Complete or incomplete? ʿalima llāhu taʿālā; ṣāra al-ʿāṣī mustaḥiqqan li-l-ʿadhābi; tuqbalu al-tawbatu.
tasks.arabic: عَلِمَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى — صَارَ الْعَاصِي مُسْتَحِقًّا لِلْعَذَابِ — تُقْبَلُ التَّوْبَةُ
tasks.answer: ʿAlima: complete; the statement is whole with its doer. Ṣāra: incomplete; it needs the khabar mustaḥiqqan in naṣb. Tuqbalu: complete; a passive verb with its deputy of the doer, al-tawbatu.

tasks.prompt: Give the noun and the khabar of the incomplete verb in tuqbalu al-tawbatu mā dāma al-rūḥu dākhilan fī al-badani, and translate.
tasks.arabic: مَا دَامَ الرُّوحُ دَاخِلًا فِي الْبَدَنِ
tasks.answer: The incomplete verb is mā dāma: its noun al-rūḥu (rafʿ), its khabar dākhilan (naṣb). “Repentance is accepted as long as the soul is within the body.”

tasks.prompt: How does Birgivī's treatment of kāna differ from the Ājurrūmiyya's?
tasks.answer: The Ājurrūmiyya puts kāna and its sisters among the words that enter the subject and predicate. Birgivī counts them as verbs under the rule that every verb governs, and calls them incomplete because their noun in rafʿ is not enough without a khabar in naṣb.

quiz.prompt: What is the first analogical governor?
quiz.explanation: Every verb gives rafʿ and naṣb.

quiz.prompt: Does an intransitive verb give naṣb at all?
options: Yes: to its maṣdar, a time, a place, a state
quiz.explanation: Nazala al-qurʾānu nuzūlan.

quiz.prompt: What makes a verb incomplete (nāqiṣ)?
options: It needs a khabar in naṣb besides its noun in rafʿ
quiz.explanation: Kāna llāhu ʿalīman.

quiz.prompt: In laysa llāhu taʿālā jisman, jisman is…
options: the khabar of laysa, in naṣb
quiz.explanation: Laysa is an incomplete verb.

quiz.prompt: “Every verb must have…”
quiz.explanation: Its doer, its deputy, or its noun.

quiz.prompt: ʿAlima llāhu taʿālā is…
options: a complete verb with its doer
quiz.explanation: The statement is whole with the noun in rafʿ.

quiz.prompt: Mā zāla al-mudhnibu baʿīdan means…
options: The sinner is no longer far
quiz.explanation: Mā zāla: “did not cease to be”.

text.original: وَالْقِيَاسِيُّ تِسْعَةٌ: الْأَوَّلُ الْفِعْلُ مُطْلَقًا، فَكُلُّ فِعْلٍ يَرْفَعُ وَيَنْصِبُ، نَحْوُ: خَلَقَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى كُلَّ شَيْءٍ، وَنَزَلَ الْقُرْآنُ نُزُولًا. وَلَا بُدَّ لِكُلِّ فِعْلٍ مِنْ مَرْفُوعٍ، فَإِنْ تَمَّ بِهِ كَلَامًا يُسَمَّى فِعْلًا تَامًّا، نَحْوُ: عَلِمَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى.
text.en: The analogical are nine. The first is the verb, without restriction: every verb puts in rafʿ and in naṣb, as khalaqa Allāhu taʿālā kulla shayʾin “God Most High created everything” and wa-nazala al-qurʾānu nuzūlan “and the Qurʾān came down, a coming down”. Every verb must have a word in rafʿ: if it is complete speech with it, it is called a complete verb (fiʿl tāmm), as ʿalima Allāhu taʿālā “God Most High knew”.

text.original: وَإِنْ لَمْ يَتِمَّ بِهِ بَلِ احْتَاجَ إِلَى خَبَرٍ مَنْصُوبٍ يُسَمَّى فِعْلًا نَاقِصًا، نَحْوُ: كَانَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى عَلِيمًا حَكِيمًا، وَصَارَ الْعَاصِي مُسْتَحِقًّا لِلْعَذَابِ، وَمَا زَالَ الْمُذْنِبُ بَعِيدًا مِنَ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى، وَتُقْبَلُ التَّوْبَةُ مَا دَامَ الرُّوحُ دَاخِلًا فِي الْبَدَنِ، وَلَيْسَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى جِسْمًا.
text.en: If it is not complete with it but needs a khabar in naṣb, it is called an incomplete verb (fiʿl nāqiṣ), as kāna Allāhu taʿālā ʿalīman ḥakīman “God Most High is ever Knowing, Wise”, wa-ṣāra al-ʿāṣī mustaḥiqqan li-al-ʿadhābi “and the disobedient became deserving of punishment”, wa-mā zāla al-mudhnibu baʿīdan mina Allāhi taʿālā “and the sinner has not ceased to be far from God Most High”, wa-tuqbalu al-tawbatu mā dāma al-rūḥu dākhilan fī al-badani “and repentance is accepted as long as the soul is within the body”, and wa-laysa Allāhu taʿālā jisman “and God Most High is not a body”.

lessons.title: The words that work like their verb
body: The next five analogical governors are nouns that work as their verbs work. The active participle (ism al-fāʿil) does the work of its active verb: kullu ḥasūdin muḥriqun ḥasaduhu ʿamalahu, “every envier, his envy burns up his deeds”. Muḥriqun, the participle of aḥraqa, “to burn”, gives rafʿ to ḥasaduhu, its doer, and naṣb to ʿamalahu, its object, exactly as yuḥriqu would.

The passive participle (ism al-mafʿūl) does the work of its passive verb: kullu tāʾibin maqbūlatun tawbatuhu, “every repenter, his repentance is accepted”. Maqbūlatun gives rafʿ to tawbatuhu, the deputy of the doer, as tuqbalu would; it is feminine because tawba is. The adjective like the participle (al-ṣifa al-mushabbaha), which names a lasting quality, does the same: al-ʿibādatu ḥasanun thawābuhā, “worship, its reward is fine”; al-maʿṣiyatu qabīḥun ʿadhābuhā, “sin, its punishment is foul”: ḥasan and qabīḥ give rafʿ to the noun after them.

The elative (ism al-tafḍīl) works too, but only in a narrow case: mā min rajulin aḥsana fīhi al-ḥilmu minhu fī al-ʿālimi, “there is no man in whom forbearance is finer than it is in the scholar”. Aḥsana gives rafʿ to the visible noun al-ḥilmu, which an elative does only in a sentence of this shape, negated and comparing a thing with itself in two places; the grammarians know it as the case of al-kuḥl, after their standard example.

The maṣdar works like its verb: yuḥibbu llāhu taʿālā iʿṭāʾahu ʿabdahu faqīran dirhaman, “God Most High loves his giving his servant, poor, a dirham”. Iʿṭāʾ, the maṣdar of aʿṭā, “to give”, takes two objects as its verb does, ʿabdahu and dirhaman; the -hu joined to it names the giver; faqīran describes the servant's state. The madrasa reads the sentence as a lesson in charity as well.
What joins these five: each is a noun made from a verb, and each keeps some of the verb's power. The Amthila taught their forms; the ʿAwāmil teaches what they do.

tasks.answer: Governor: muḥriqun, the active participle of aḥraqa. In rafʿ: ḥasaduhu, its doer. In naṣb: ʿamalahu, its object. “Every envier, his envy burns up his deeds.”

tasks.prompt: Why is maqbūlatun feminine in kullu tāʾibin maqbūlatun tawbatuhu, though tāʾib is masculine?
tasks.arabic: كُلُّ تَائِبٍ مَقْبُولَةٌ تَوْبَتُهُ
tasks.answer: The passive participle works like its verb, and a verb agrees with the noun it governs in rafʿ: here tawbatuhu, “his repentance”, which is feminine (as tuqbalu tawbatuhu).

tasks.prompt: What do ḥasanun and qabīḥun govern in al-ʿibādatu ḥasanun thawābuhā wa-l-maʿṣiyatu qabīḥun ʿadhābuhā?

tasks.answer: Each is an adjective like the participle and gives rafʿ to the noun after it: ḥasanun to thawābuhā, qabīḥun to ʿadhābuhā.

tasks.prompt: Which of the five works only in a narrow case, and what is that case?

text.original: وَالثَّانِي اسْمُ الْفَاعِلِ، فَهُوَ يَعْمَلُ عَمَلَ فِعْلِهِ الْمَعْلُومِ، نَحْوُ: كُلُّ حَسُودٍ مُحْرِقٌ حَسَدُهُ عَمَلَهُ. وَالثَّالِثُ اسْمُ الْمَفْعُولِ، فَهُوَ يَعْمَلُ عَمَلَ فِعْلِهِ الْمَجْهُولِ، نَحْوُ: كُلُّ تَائِبٍ مَقْبُولَةٌ تَوْبَتُهُ. وَالرَّابِعُ الصِّفَةُ الْمُشَبَّهَةُ، فَهِيَ أَيْضًا تَعْمَلُ عَمَلَ فِعْلِهَا، نَحْوُ: الْعِبَادَةُ حَسَنٌ ثَوَابُهَا، وَالْمَعْصِيَةُ قَبِيحٌ عَذَابُهَا.
text.en: The second is the active participle (ism al-fāʿil): it governs as its active verb governs, as kullu ḥasūdin muḥriqun ḥasaduhu ʿamalahu “every envious man, his envy burns up his deeds”. The third is the passive participle (ism al-mafʿūl): it governs as its passive verb governs, as kullu tāʾibin maqbūlatun tawbatuhu “every penitent, his repentance is accepted”. The fourth is the adjective like the participle (al-ṣifa al-mushabbaha): it too governs as its verb governs, as al-ʿibādatu ḥasanun thawābuhā “worship, its reward is good” and wa-al-maʿṣiyatu qabīḥun ʿadhābuhā “and disobedience, its punishment is ugly”.

text.original: وَالْخَامِسُ اسْمُ التَّفْضِيلِ، فَهُوَ أَيْضًا يَعْمَلُ عَمَلَ فِعْلِهِ، نَحْوُ: مَا مِنْ رَجُلٍ أَحْسَنَ فِيهِ الْحِلْمُ مِنْهُ فِي الْعَالِمِ. وَالسَّادِسُ الْمَصْدَرُ، فَهُوَ أَيْضًا يَعْمَلُ عَمَلَ فِعْلِهِ، نَحْوُ: يُحِبُّ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى إِعْطَاءَهُ عَبْدَهُ فَقِيرًا دِرْهَمًا.
text.en: The fifth is the elative (ism al-tafḍīl): it too governs as its verb governs, as mā min rajulin aḥsana fīhi al-ḥilmu minhu fī al-ʿālimi “there is no man in whom forbearance is finer than it is in the scholar”. The sixth is the maṣdar: it too governs as its verb governs, as yuḥibbu Allāhu taʿālā iʿṭāʾahu ʿabdahu faqīran dirhaman “God Most High loves his giving his servant, poor [as he is], a dirham”.

lessons.title: The muḍāf, the vague noun, the meaning of the verb; the abstract governors
lessons.arabic: الْمُضَافُ وَالْمُبْهَمُ وَمَعْنَى الْفِعْلِ وَالْعَامِلُ الْمَعْنَوِيُّ
lessons.transliteration: al-muḍāf wa-l-mubham wa-maʿnā al-fiʿl wa-l-ʿāmil al-maʿnawī
body: The seventh analogical governor is the noun joined to another (al-muḍāf), which puts the second in jarr: ʿibādatu llāhi taʿālā khayrun, “the worship of God Most High is good”. Here ʿibāda is the governor of Allāh. The Ājurrūmiyya spoke of the noun “in khafḍ by iḍāfa”; Birgivī names the first term itself as the governor.

The eighth is the complete vague noun (al-ism al-mubham al-tāmm), which puts its tamyīz in naṣb: al-tarāwīḥu ʿishrūna rakʿatan, “the tarāwīḥ prayer is twenty rakʿas”. ʿIshrūna is vague, twenty of what?, and complete, ending in its nūn, so it governs rakʿatan in naṣb. The example is a point of Ḥanafī fiqh, the twenty rakʿas of the night prayer of Ramaḍān, put into a lesson on numbers.

The ninth is the meaning of the verb (maʿnā al-fiʿl): “every word from which the meaning of a verb is understood”. Hayhāta al-mudhnibu min allāhi taʿālā, “how far the sinner is from God!”: hayhāta means “it is far” and gives rafʿ to al-mudhnibu. Tarāki dhanban, “leave sin!”: tarāki means “leave!” and gives naṣb to dhanban. Mā fī al-dunyā rāḥatun, “there is no rest in this world”: fī al-dunyā carries the meaning of “is found”, and the commentaries read rāḥatun as governed by it. And yanbaghī li-l-ʿālimi an yakūna muḥammadiyyan khuluquhu, “the scholar should be one whose character is Muḥammadan”: the relative adjective muḥammadiyyan, “related to Muḥammad”, gives rafʿ to khuluquhu.

The two abstract governors close the sixty. The first is “the raiser of the subject and the predicate”: Muḥammadun rasūlu llāhi, where no word stands before Muḥammad; his being put first is what governs. The second is “the raiser of the present verb”: yarḥamu llāhu taʿālā al-tāʾiba, “God Most High has mercy on the one who repents”, where yarḥamu is in rafʿ because no governor of naṣb or jazm has entered on it.
With these the first chapter is done: forty-nine heard governors, nine analogical, two abstract. A student who can name the governor of every word in Birgivī's sentences has learnt the chapter.

tasks.prompt: Name the governor of the second word in each, and the state it gives: ʿibādatu llāhi; ʿishrūna rakʿatan; hayhāta al-mudhnibu; tarāki dhanban.
tasks.arabic: عِبَادَةُ اللَّهِ — عِشْرُونَ رَكْعَةً — هَيْهَاتَ الْمُذْنِبُ — تَرَاكِ ذَنْبًا
tasks.answer: Llāhi: ʿibāda, the muḍāf (jarr). Rakʿatan: ʿishrūna, the complete vague noun (naṣb as tamyīz). Al-mudhnibu: hayhāta, a noun meaning “it is far” (rafʿ as its doer). Dhanban: tarāki, a noun meaning “leave!” (naṣb as its object).

tasks.prompt: Why is ʿishrūna called “vague” and “complete”?
tasks.arabic: عِشْرُونَ
tasks.answer: Vague, because “twenty” says nothing of what is counted until the tamyīz comes. Complete, because it ends in its nūn and is not joined to a following word; so it puts the tamyīz in naṣb.

tasks.prompt: What governs Muḥammadun in Muḥammadun rasūlu llāhi, and yarḥamu in yarḥamu llāhu taʿālā al-tāʾiba?
tasks.arabic: مُحَمَّدٌ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ — يَرْحَمُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى التَّائِبَ
tasks.answer: Both are governed by abstract governors. Muḥammadun: its being put first to be spoken of (which governs subject and predicate). Yarḥamu: its being free of every governor of naṣb and jazm.

tasks.prompt: In yanbaghī li-l-ʿālimi an yakūna muḥammadiyyan khuluquhu, what does muḥammadiyyan govern, and why can it?
tasks.arabic: أَنْ يَكُونَ مُحَمَّدِيًّا خُلُقُهُ
tasks.answer: It gives rafʿ to khuluquhu. Muḥammadiyyan is a relative adjective, meaning “related to Muḥammad”; a verb's meaning is understood from it, and so it governs by the meaning of the verb.

quiz.explanation: Birgivī names the first term of the iḍāfa as the governor.

quiz.explanation: ʿIshrūna rakʿatan.

quiz.prompt: What does hayhāta mean?
quiz.explanation: It gives rafʿ to al-mudhnibu as its doer.

quiz.explanation: Tarāki, a noun with the meaning of “leave!”, gives naṣb to dhanban.

quiz.prompt: How many abstract governors are there?

text.original: وَالسَّابِعُ الِاسْمُ الْمُضَافُ، فَهُوَ يَعْمَلُ الْجَرَّ، نَحْوُ: عِبَادَةُ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى خَيْرٌ. وَالثَّامِنُ الِاسْمُ الْمُبْهَمُ التَّامُّ، فَهُوَ يَعْمَلُ النَّصْبَ، نَحْوُ: التَّرَاوِيحُ عِشْرُونَ رَكْعَةً.
text.en: The seventh is the muḍāf noun: it governs jarr, as ʿibādatu Allāhi taʿālā khayrun “the worship of God Most High is good”. The eighth is the complete vague noun (al-ism al-mubham al-tāmm): it governs naṣb, as al-tarāwīḥu ʿishrūna rakʿatan “the tarāwīḥ are twenty rakʿas”.

text.original: وَالتَّاسِعُ مَعْنَى الْفِعْلِ، أَيْ كُلُّ لَفْظٍ يُفْهَمُ مِنْهُ مَعْنَى فِعْلٍ، نَحْوُ: هَيْهَاتَ الْمُذْنِبُ مِنَ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى، وَتَرَاكِ ذَنْبًا، وَنَحْوُ: مَا فِي الدُّنْيَا رَاحَةٌ، وَنَحْوُ: يَنْبَغِي لِلْعَالِمِ أَنْ يَكُونَ مُحَمَّدِيًّا خُلُقُهُ.
text.en: The ninth is the meaning of the verb (maʿnā al-fiʿl), that is, every word from which the meaning of a verb is understood, as hayhāta al-mudhnibu mina Allāhi taʿālā “how far the sinner is from God Most High!” and wa-tarāki dhanban “and leave sin!”; and as mā fī al-dunyā rāḥatun “there is no rest in this world”; and as yanbaghī li-al-ʿālimi an yakūna muḥammadiyyan khuluquhu “the scholar should be one whose character is like Muḥammad's”.

text.original: وَالْمَعْنَوِيُّ اثْنَانِ: الْأَوَّلُ رَافِعُ الْمُبْتَدَإِ وَالْخَبَرِ، نَحْوُ: مُحَمَّدٌ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ، وَالثَّانِي رَافِعُ الْفِعْلِ الْمُضَارِعِ، نَحْوُ: يَرْحَمُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى التَّائِبَ.
text.en: The abstract are two. The first is what puts the mubtadaʾ and the khabar in rafʿ, as Muḥammadun rasūlu Allāhi “Muḥammad is the Messenger of God”; the second is what puts the muḍāriʿ verb in rafʿ, as yarḥamu Allāhu taʿālā al-tāʾiba “God Most High has mercy on the penitent”.

lessons.title: The governed word; the nine in rafʿ
body: The second chapter turns from the governors to the words they govern, and sorts them first in two. Some are governed in their own right (bi-l-aṣāla): a governor acts on them directly. Others are governed by following (bi-l-tabaʿiyya): “their iʿrāb is like the iʿrāb of what they follow”, the adjective, the conjunction and the rest. The first kind is of four sorts: in rafʿ, in naṣb, in jarr (nouns only), and in jazm (verbs only).

Nine are in rafʿ. The doer: raḥima llāhu taʿālā al-tāʾiba, “God Most High had mercy on the one who repents”. The deputy of the doer: ruḥima al-tāʾibu, “the one who repents was shown mercy”. The subject and the predicate: Muḥammadun khātamu al-anbiyāʾi, “Muḥammad is the seal of the prophets”. The noun of kāna and its sisters: kāna llāhu taʿālā ʿalīman ḥakīman.

The predicate of inna and its sisters: inna al-baʿtha ḥaqqun, “the resurrection is true”. The predicate of the lā of the kind: lā ʿamala murāʾin maqbūlun, “no deed of a show-off is accepted”. The noun of mā and lā like laysa: mā al-takabburu lāʾiqan li-l-ʿālimi, “pride does not befit the scholar”, wa-lā ḥasadun ḥalālan, “and no envy is lawful”. And the present verb free of the governors of naṣb and jazm: yuḥibbu llāhu taʿālā al-tawāḍuʿa, “God Most High loves humility”.

Set the list beside the seven of the Ājurrūmiyya. Birgivī adds three: the predicate of the lā of the kind and the noun of mā and lā like laysa, because he counted those governors, and the present verb in rafʿ, because his governed words include verbs. The followers he leaves for the end of the chapter, as the second kind. Each item here is the other face of a governor of chapter one: the doer of the verb, the predicate of inna, the noun of mā.

tasks.arabic: مُحَمَّدٌ خَاتَمُ الْأَنْبِيَاءِ — إِنَّ الْبَعْثَ حَقٌّ — مَا التَّكَبُّرُ لَائِقًا لِلْعَالِمِ
tasks.answer: Muḥammadun: the subject; khātamu: the predicate. Ḥaqqun: the predicate of inna. Al-takabburu: the noun of mā like laysa.

tasks.prompt: Find the two words in rafʿ in yuḥibbu llāhu taʿālā al-tawāḍuʿa, and name the governor of each.
tasks.arabic: يُحِبُّ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى التَّوَاضُعَ
tasks.answer: Yuḥibbu, the present verb, in rafʿ by its freedom from every governor of naṣb and jazm (an abstract governor). Llāhu, its doer, in rafʿ by the verb.

tasks.prompt: What is the difference between a word governed in its own right and one governed by following?
tasks.answer: A word governed in its own right has a governor that acts on it directly (the doer by its verb). A word governed by following has the iʿrāb of the word it follows (an adjective takes the state of its noun).

tasks.prompt: Which three words in rafʿ does Birgivī have that the Ājurrūmiyya's seven do not, and why?
tasks.answer: The predicate of the lā of the kind, the noun of mā and lā like laysa, and the present verb in rafʿ. He counted those governors in chapter one, and his governed words include verbs as well as nouns.

quiz.prompt: How many words in rafʿ does Birgivī count?
quiz.explanation: He adds three to the seven of the Ājurrūmiyya.

quiz.explanation: The passive verb leaves the doer unnamed.

quiz.explanation: The lā of the kind: noun in naṣb, predicate in rafʿ.

quiz.explanation: Mā like laysa: noun in rafʿ, khabar in naṣb.

text.original: وَهُوَ عَلَى ضَرْبَيْنِ: مَعْمُولٌ بِالْأَصَالَةِ، وَمَعْمُولٌ بِالتَّبَعِيَّةِ، أَيْ إِعْرَابُهُ يَكُونُ مِثْلَ إِعْرَابِ مَتْبُوعِهِ. الضَّرْبُ الْأَوَّلُ أَرْبَعَةُ أَنْوَاعٍ: مَرْفُوعٌ، وَمَنْصُوبٌ، وَمَجْرُورٌ مُخْتَصٌّ بِالِاسْمِ، وَمَجْزُومٌ مُخْتَصٌّ بِالْفِعْلِ.
text.en: It is of two kinds: governed in itself (bi-l-aṣāla) and governed by following (bi-l-tabaʿiyya), that is, its iʿrāb is like the iʿrāb of the word it follows. The first kind is of four sorts: marfūʿ; manṣūb; majrūr, which belongs to the noun only; and majzūm, which belongs to the verb only.

text.original: أَمَّا الْمَرْفُوعُ فَتِسْعَةٌ: الْأَوَّلُ الْفَاعِلُ، نَحْوُ: رَحِمَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى التَّائِبَ. وَالثَّانِي نَائِبُ الْفَاعِلِ، نَحْوُ: رُحِمَ التَّائِبُ. وَالثَّالِثُ الْمُبْتَدَأُ، وَالرَّابِعُ الْخَبَرُ، نَحْوُ: مُحَمَّدٌ خَاتَمُ الْأَنْبِيَاءِ عَلَيْهِمُ الصَّلَاةُ وَالسَّلَامُ. وَالْخَامِسُ اسْمُ بَابِ كَانَ وَأَخَوَاتِهَا، نَحْوُ: كَانَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى عَلِيمًا حَكِيمًا.
text.en: As for the marfūʿ, it is nine. The first is the fāʿil, as raḥima Allāhu taʿālā al-tāʾiba “God Most High had mercy on the penitent”. The second is the deputy of the doer (nāʾib al-fāʿil), as ruḥima al-tāʾibu “the penitent was shown mercy”. The third is the mubtadaʾ, and the fourth the khabar, as Muḥammadun khātamu al-anbiyāʾi ʿalayhimu al-ṣalātu wa-al-salāmu “Muḥammad is the seal of the prophets, upon them be blessing and peace”. The fifth is the noun of the class of kāna and its sisters, as kāna Allāhu taʿālā ʿalīman ḥakīman “God Most High is ever Knowing, Wise”.

text.original: وَالسَّادِسُ خَبَرُ بَابِ إِنَّ، نَحْوُ: إِنَّ الْبَعْثَ حَقٌّ. وَالسَّابِعُ خَبَرُ لَا لِنَفْيِ الْجِنْسِ، نَحْوُ: لَا عَمَلَ مُرَاءٍ مَقْبُولٌ. وَالثَّامِنُ اسْمُ مَا وَلَا الْمُشَبَّهَتَيْنِ بِلَيْسَ، نَحْوُ: مَا التَّكَبُّرُ لَائِقًا لِلْعَالِمِ، وَلَا حَسَدٌ حَلَالًا. وَالتَّاسِعُ الْفِعْلُ الْمُضَارِعُ الْخَالِي عَنِ النَّوَاصِبِ وَالْجَوَازِمِ، نَحْوُ: يُحِبُّ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى التَّوَاضُعَ.
text.en: The sixth is the khabar of the class of inna, as inna al-baʿtha ḥaqqun “indeed the resurrection is true”. The seventh is the khabar of the lā that denies the whole kind, as lā ʿamala murāʾin maqbūlun “no deed of one who shows off is accepted”. The eighth is the noun of mā and lā that resemble laysa, as mā al-takabburu lāʾiqan li-al-ʿālimi “pride is not fitting for a scholar” and wa-lā ḥasadun ḥalālan “and no envy is lawful”. The ninth is the muḍāriʿ verb free of the nawāṣib and the jawāzim, as yuḥibbu Allāhu taʿālā al-tawāḍuʿa “God Most High loves humility”.

lessons.title: The words in naṣb (1): the five objects and more
body: Thirteen are in naṣb, and Birgivī starts with the five objects, under the names the later books use. The absolute object (al-mafʿūl al-muṭlaq): tubtu tawbatan naṣūḥan, “I have repented a sincere repentance”. The object (al-mafʿūl bihi): uʿbudi llāha taʿālā, “worship God Most High”. The object in which (al-mafʿūl fīhi), the adverb of time or place: ṣum shahra ramaḍāna, “fast the month of Ramaḍān”. The object for which (al-mafʿūl lahu): iʿmal ṭalaban li-marḍāti llāhi taʿālā, “act seeking the good pleasure of God Most High”. The object with which (al-mafʿūl maʿahu): yafnā al-mālu wa-tabqā wa-ʿamalaka, “wealth perishes, and you remain, with your deeds”.

In the last example the wāw before ʿamalaka means “with”: you remain together with your deeds, and so ʿamalaka is in naṣb. Our print is not clear at this point; the sentence is read from an Ottoman lithograph of the same book.

Then five more. The state (ḥāl): uʿbudi llāha taʿālā khāʾifan rājiyan, “worship God Most High fearing and hoping”: two states of the worshipper at once. The specification (tamyīz): ṭāba al-ʿālimu ʿibādatan, “the scholar is good in worship”. The excepted (mustathnā): yadkhulu al-jannata al-nāsu illā al-kāfira, “people enter Paradise, except the unbeliever”. The predicate of kāna: kāna al-malāʾikatu ʿibāda llāhi, “the angels were servants of God”. The noun of inna: inna al-suʾāla ḥaqqun, “the questioning (in the grave) is true”.

Two details for the careful reader. In yadkhulu al-jannata al-nāsu, the object al-jannata comes before the doer al-nāsu: word order is free, and only the endings show who does what. And in kāna al-malāʾikatu, the verb is masculine and singular before a plural of angels; a broken plural may take such a verb. Each sentence again teaches belief: sincere repentance, fear and hope, the questioning in the grave.

terms.en: the absolute object: tawbatan
the object in which: the adverb
the object for which: the reason
the object with which: after the wāw of “with”
the state: khāʾifan rājiyan

examples.en: tubtu tawbatan naṣūḥan, “I have repented a sincere repentance”: the absolute object
ṣum shahra ramaḍāna, “fast the month of Ramaḍān”: the object in which
yafnā al-mālu wa-tabqā wa-ʿamalaka: the object with which, after the wāw of “with”
uʿbudi llāha taʿālā khāʾifan rājiyan, “worship God fearing and hoping”: two ḥāls
yadkhulu al-jannata al-nāsu illā al-kāfira: the object before the doer, and the excepted in naṣb

tasks.prompt: Name the word in naṣb and its kind: iʿmal ṭalaban li-marḍāti llāhi taʿālā; ṭāba al-ʿālimu ʿibādatan; inna al-suʾāla ḥaqqun.
tasks.arabic: اعْمَلْ طَلَبًا لِمَرْضَاةِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى — طَابَ الْعَالِمُ عِبَادَةً — إِنَّ السُّؤَالَ حَقٌّ
tasks.answer: Ṭalaban: the object for which (why act? seeking God's pleasure). ʿIbādatan: the specification (good in what respect? in worship). Al-suʾāla: the noun of inna.

tasks.prompt: In yadkhulu al-jannata al-nāsu illā al-kāfira, which word is the doer, which the object, and how do you know?
tasks.arabic: يَدْخُلُ الْجَنَّةَ النَّاسُ إِلَّا الْكَافِرَ
tasks.answer: Al-nāsu is the doer (rafʿ, ḍamma); al-jannata is the object (naṣb, fatḥa), though it comes first. The endings show the roles; al-kāfira is the excepted, in naṣb.

tasks.prompt: Explain the naṣb of ʿamalaka in yafnā al-mālu wa-tabqā wa-ʿamalaka.
tasks.arabic: وَتَبْقَى وَعَمَلَكَ
tasks.answer: The wāw means “with”: you remain together with your deeds. The noun after this wāw is the object with which (mafʿūl maʿahu), in naṣb.

tasks.prompt: In uʿbudi llāha taʿālā khāʾifan rājiyan, whose state do khāʾifan and rājiyan describe, and what do they answer?
tasks.arabic: اعْبُدِ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى خَائِفًا رَاجِيًا
tasks.answer: The state of the one addressed, the doer of uʿbud (“you”). They answer “how?”: fearing and hoping at once.

quiz.explanation: The maṣdar of the verb, with its adjective naṣūḥan.

quiz.explanation: ʿIbāda, in naṣb, joined to llāhi.

quiz.prompt: Uʿbudi llāha khāʾifan rājiyan has…
quiz.explanation: Fearing and hoping: two states at once.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْمَنْصُوبُ فَثَلَاثَةَ عَشَرَ: الْأَوَّلُ الْمَفْعُولُ الْمُطْلَقُ، نَحْوُ: تُبْتُ تَوْبَةً نَصُوحًا. وَالثَّانِي الْمَفْعُولُ بِهِ، نَحْوُ: اعْبُدِ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى. وَالثَّالِثُ الْمَفْعُولُ فِيهِ، نَحْوُ: صُمْ شَهْرَ رَمَضَانَ. وَالرَّابِعُ الْمَفْعُولُ لَهُ، نَحْوُ: اعْمَلْ طَلَبًا لِمَرْضَاةِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى. وَالْخَامِسُ الْمَفْعُولُ مَعَهُ، نَحْوُ: يَفْنَى الْمَالُ وَتَبْقَى وَعَمَلَكَ.
text.en: As for the manṣūb, it is thirteen. The first is the absolute object (al-mafʿūl al-muṭlaq), as tubtu tawbatan naṣūḥan “I repented with a sincere repentance”. The second is the direct object (al-mafʿūl bihi), as uʿbudi Allāha taʿālā “worship God Most High”. The third is the adverb (al-mafʿūl fīhi), as ṣum shahra Ramaḍāna “fast the month of Ramaḍān”. The fourth is the object of purpose (al-mafʿūl lahu), as iʿmal ṭalaban li-marḍāti Allāhi taʿālā “act, seeking the good pleasure of God Most High”. The fifth is the object of accompaniment (al-mafʿūl maʿahu), as yafnā al-mālu wa-tabqā wa-ʿamalaka “wealth passes away, and you remain with your deeds”.

text.original: وَالسَّادِسُ الْحَالُ، نَحْوُ: اعْبُدِ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى خَائِفًا رَاجِيًا. وَالسَّابِعُ التَّمْيِيزُ، نَحْوُ: طَابَ الْعَالِمُ عِبَادَةً. وَالثَّامِنُ الْمُسْتَثْنَى، نَحْوُ: يَدْخُلُ الْجَنَّةَ النَّاسُ إِلَّا الْكَافِرَ. وَالتَّاسِعُ خَبَرُ بَابِ كَانَ، نَحْوُ: كَانَ الْمَلَائِكَةُ عِبَادَ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى. وَالْعَاشِرُ اسْمُ بَابِ إِنَّ، نَحْوُ: إِنَّ السُّؤَالَ حَقٌّ.
text.en: The sixth is the ḥāl, as uʿbudi Allāha taʿālā khāʾifan rājiyan “worship God Most High fearing and hoping”. The seventh is the tamyīz, as ṭāba al-ʿālimu ʿibādatan “the scholar was good in worship”. The eighth is the mustathnā, as yadkhulu al-jannata al-nāsu illā al-kāfira “the people enter Paradise, except the unbeliever”. The ninth is the khabar of the class of kāna, as kāna al-malāʾikatu ʿibāda Allāhi taʿālā “the angels were the servants of God Most High”. The tenth is the noun of the class of inna, as inna al-suʾāla ḥaqqun “indeed the questioning [in the grave] is true”.

lessons.title: The words in naṣb (2); in jarr; in jazm
body: Three more words in naṣb complete the thirteen. The noun of the lā of the kind: lā ṭāʿata mughtābin maqbūlatun, “no obedience of a backbiter is accepted”. The predicate of mā and lā like laysa: mā al-ghībatu ḥalālan, “backbiting is not lawful”, wa-lā namīmatun jāʾizatan, “and no tale-bearing is permitted”. And the present verb with a governor of naṣb: uḥibbu an tughfara dhunūbī, “I love that my sins be forgiven”.

The words in jarr are two: the noun in jarr by a particle, iʿmal bi-ikhlāṣin, “act with sincerity”; and the noun in jarr by iḍāfa, dhanbu al-ʿabdi yusawwidu qalbahu, “the servant's sin blackens his heart”. And the word in jazm is one: the present verb with a governor of jazm, in tukhliṣ yuqbal ʿamaluka, “if you are sincere, your deed will be accepted”.

Count the governed words in their own right: nine in rafʿ, thirteen in naṣb, two in jarr, one in jazm: twenty-five. With the five followers of the next lesson they make the thirty that the opening promised.

Notice how one governor of chapter one appears twice here. The lā of the kind gives its noun naṣb (this lesson) and its predicate rafʿ (lesson 10); mā and lā like laysa give their noun rafʿ (lesson 10) and their predicate naṣb (this lesson). Learning the governed words is learning the governors again from the other side, and the madrasa often recites the two chapters side by side.

the predicate of mā and lā like laysa, in naṣb
in jarr by a particle

the verb in jazm

mā al-ghībatu ḥalālan, “backbiting is not lawful”: the predicate of mā in naṣb
